{{Short description|Theorem in probability theory}}
{{one source|date=June 2010}}
In [[geometric probability]] theory, '''Wendel's theorem''', named after James G. Wendel, gives the [[probability]] that ''N'' points [[continuous uniform distribution|distributed uniformly]] at random on an [[n-sphere|<math>n</math>-dimensional hypersphere]] all lie on the same "half" of the hypersphere.  In other words, one seeks the probability that there is some [[Half-space (geometry)|half-space]] with the origin on its boundary that contains all ''N'' points.  Wendel's theorem says that the probability is<ref>{{citation
|last = Wendel|first = James G.|title = A Problem in Geometric Probability|journal = Math. Scand.|volume = 11|year = 1962|pages = 109–111| doi=10.7146/math.scand.a-10655 |url = http://www.mscand.dk/article/view/10655}}</ref>
: <math> p_{n,N}=2^{-N+1}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\binom{N-1}{k}. </math>

The statement is equivalent to <math> p_{n,N}</math> being the probability that the origin is not contained in the [[convex hull]] of the ''N'' points and holds for any probability distribution on {{math|'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>}} that is symmetric around the origin. In particular this includes all distribution which are [[rotational invariance|rotationally invariant]] around the origin.

This is essentially a probabilistic restatement of [[Ludwig Schläfli|Schläfli]]'s theorem that <math>N</math> hyperplanes in general position in <math>\R^n</math> divides it into <math> 2\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\binom{N-1}{k} </math> regions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cover |first1=Thomas M. |last2=Efron |first2=Bradley |date=February 1967 |title=Geometrical Probability and Random Points on a Hypersphere |journal=The Annals of Mathematical Statistics |volume=38 |issue=1 |pages=213–220 |doi=10.1214/aoms/1177699073 |issn=0003-4851|doi-access=free }}</ref>
